name: Shea butter
lead: Shea butter is a fat extracted from the nuts of the shea tree (Vitellaria paradoxa), which grows wild across the dry savanna belt of West and Central Africa. It is mainly a triglyceride fat rich in oleic and stearic acids, ivory in colour when unrefined.[1][2]

It is used in cooking in parts of Africa, as a cocoa-butter substitute in confectionery, and in cosmetics as an emollient and skin conditioner, including in moisturizers, lotions, soaps and hair products.[1][2] Traditional use for dry skin, burns and rashes is documented in ethnomedical accounts.[2]

Evidence for specific cosmetic claims is limited: laboratory studies have examined its anti-inflammatory triterpenes, and small trials have tested shea-containing products, but no trial found tests shea butter alone for appearance outcomes.[3][4]

paras: The fat contains five main fatty acids (palmitic, stearic, oleic, linoleic and arachidic); stearic and oleic acids make up roughly 85 to 90 percent, with stearic giving firmness and oleic softness. Composition varies by region, with Ugandan butter higher in oleic acid and Burkina Faso butter tending to be harder.[1] A 2014 review identified ten phenolic compounds, eight of them catechins.[1]

Traditional production, carried out largely by women in rural communities, involves collecting fruits, removing the pulp, cracking and processing the kernels, and churning the butter.[2] Commercial grades run from A (raw, unrefined, water-extracted) through B (refined) to C (highly refined, solvent-extracted, white); Wikipedia states refining can remove up to 95 percent of vitamin content.[1] Grokipedia reports that unsaponifiable matter such as triterpenes and sterols forms about 4 to 11 percent of the butter.[2]

In cosmetics shea butter is used mainly as an emollient and skin conditioner in moisturizers, lotions and soaps.[1] Product labels list it in items such as antiperspirant deodorant sprays.[5] It is also eaten in some African countries and blended with other oils as a cocoa butter substitute, though the taste differs noticeably.[1]

No clinical trial found tests shea butter on its own for appearance outcomes. Registered studies have tested combination products containing shea butter, such as a cream with spent grain wax extract, argan oil and shea butter after a trichloroacetic acid peel[6] and the same combination in acne,[7] and a moisturizing lotion in atopic eczema.[8]

Laboratory research has examined triterpene cinnamates and acetates from shea fat for anti-inflammatory and chemopreventive activity,[9] and a review of topical plant oils discusses effects on skin inflammation and barrier repair for several oils.[3] Studies of dietary fats high in stearic acid concern blood lipids and are not about skin.[10]

The English word "shea" derives from the Bambara name for the tree. A seed coat found at the medieval village of Saouga provides evidence of production by the 14th century, and the butter was being imported into Britain by 1846.[1] Grokipedia reports that in 2025 Nigeria introduced a six-month ban on raw shea nut exports to encourage local processing and that Ghana planned a phased ban by 2026; this is from an AI-generated source and unverified.[2]

card.summary: A plant fat from African shea nuts used as an emollient; supported mainly by tradition and lab data, with no solo-ingredient appearance trials.
card.note: Refined grades may retain far less of the vitamin and phenolic content than unrefined butter.

quick.overview:
Shea butter is a creamy fat from the nuts of the African shea tree. It is used as a moisturizer, in hair products, in soaps and, in some regions, as a cooking fat.

Traditional use for dry skin and burns is well documented, and lab studies show anti-inflammatory compounds in it, but no trial found tests it alone for appearance.
quick.mechanism: It acts as an emollient, softening and coating the skin with fatty acids (mainly oleic and stearic). Lab work has examined triterpenes in the unsaponifiable fraction for anti-inflammatory activity.
quick.risks: Safety assessments cited by Grokipedia describe low toxicity for skin and oral use. Highly refined grades are reported to contain much less of the vitamin and phenolic content than raw butter.
